text: Every measurement outcome in quantum mechanics is an eigenvalue, and every definite state a measurement can collapse into is an eigenvector. numpy dot linalg dot eig and eigvalsh compute both directly from a gate or observable matrix.

A vector v is an eigenvector of matrix A with eigenvalue lambda if applying A to v only scales it, never rotates it. For any 2 by 2 matrix you can solve this by hand with trace and determinant before ever touching NumPy. Pauli matrices always come out to eigenvalues plus one and minus one, exactly the two outcomes of a real qubit measurement. And when a matrix is Hermitian, which every quantum observable is, eigvalsh is the faster, numerically stable choice.

Pauli-X isn't diagonal, so its eigenvectors aren't obvious by inspection, but the hand calculation still gives eigenvalues plus one and minus one. numpy dot linalg dot eig confirms it directly: the eigenvalues array shows one and negative one, and the eigenvectors come back as the columns point seven zero seven one, point seven zero seven one and its mirror — matching the by-hand result exactly.

Take M, two one, one two, symmetric and therefore Hermitian. eigvalsh guarantees real, sorted eigenvalues using a more stable algorithm than the general-purpose eig, and here it returns one and three — confirmed separately by plugging candidate eigenvectors back into M and checking they only get scaled, not rotated.
Next lesson moves from one qubit to many: the Kronecker product, which is exactly how two 2-dimensional single-qubit vectors combine into one genuinely 4-dimensional two-qubit state.
